items.title: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
items.summary: Fear and misinformation surrounds the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo - Dr Kamwanga's mother was not immune.
items.content:
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.

They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.

"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.

But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.

This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.

Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.

Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.

After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.

"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.

The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.

The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.

After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.

Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.

This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.

After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.

This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.

"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.

Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.

He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.

"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.

In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.

Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.

"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.

Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.

The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.

However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

'I buried my parents one day after the other' - Ebola mourners learn how to grieve safely

"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.

For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.

He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.

"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.

They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.

Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.

After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.

"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."

During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.

But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.

Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.

"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".

He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.

But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.

Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.

He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."

He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing .

"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.

Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.

"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

items.title: Judo champion shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy
items.summary: Teddy Riner is one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, and one in five voters say they could support him.
items.content:
Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.

That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.

The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.

But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.

Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.

More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.

Actors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.

"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro.

"But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes."

For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly.

But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray.

The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May.

So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note.

It is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling.

Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!"

In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks.

All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices.

"People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said.

"Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool."

It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers.

Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?

France's Marine Le Pen, fighting court conviction and running for presidency

But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now.

What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform, investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine?

In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate?

Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen.

In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes.

The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off.

Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right.

The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February.

The addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely.

So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday.

The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals".

That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss.

Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist".

Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat.

If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form.

In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt.

French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104

French protests see numbers surge as unions join strikes over high cost of living

items.title: How telecoms upgrade work sparked US flight chaos
items.summary: US officials say the disruption was caused by old equipment overloading and not a cyber-attack.
items.content:
An upgrade to a decades-old telecoms network in the US caused the longest nationwide grounding of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks.

Friday's stoppage occurred when part of a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate was switched to fibre from copper wiring so old it has been discontinued, said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday.

US planes were grounded for more than four hours, affecting thousands of flights and passengers.

Earlier Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyber-attack and that everybody was safe.

On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network.

As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network.

According to Duffy, that router started flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.

As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced "instability" on voice and ground communications, said Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper.

This meant the FAA had to "pore through" the physical documents "to figure out who's working on what", Bedford admitted.

As a precaution as it tried to track down the cause, Bedford said the decision was made to ground all flights.

Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".

He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

Duffy said the system needed a complete overhaul, estimating a $50bn price tag.

In the meantime, he said authorities would work to determine whether it was "incompetence" or faulty equipment that led to the outage.

He also said there would be "re-evaluation" of allowing upgrades to be done during the day.

In a statement on Saturday afternoon, L3Harris confirmed it was working with the FAA to modernise the airspace communications infrastructure and said it was supporting the agency with its investigation.

"L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the firm said.

Juliette Kayyem, US assistant secretary of Homeland Security under President Barack Obama, questioned why an upgrade was done on one of the week's busiest days for travel.

"You don't do it on a Friday when there's lots of air traffic controllers," she said

"You try to find ways to minimise its upgrade so you're not maybe doing it across the board in a single moment but you also have to have systems that are ready to step in if the upgrade in any way begins to threaten the system," Kayyem added.

A spokesperson for L3Harris said is it "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel".

He added: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."

The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.

The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.

More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.

Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.

Have you been affected by the flight disruption? Get in touch

All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended.

There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.

Passengers travelling from the UK have been warned of possible disruption on Saturday morning.

A number of flights to the US from Heathrow airport were cancelled and delayed, but Manchester airport said no significant disruption was expected. Flights were operating as normal from Gatwick airport.

Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, had grounded all US-bound flights, but scheduled flights are now expected to depart as planned.

Air Canada also cancelled flights between the US and Canada.

But, as he predicted on Friday, it is taking time to unwind what happened.

FlightAware said more than 5,900 flights were cancelled and more than 7,000 delayed in the US on Saturday.

Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations but they both cancelled 20% of their flights on Saturday. American Airlines cancelled 520 journeys.

In the US, UK and the EU, airlines may be liable for compensation if the reason for a delay is deemed within their control, such as a fault with the plane or pilot sickness.

As such, airlines do not have to provide compensation to passengers for air traffic control problems.

But passengers are still protected to a certain degree under US federal - and country-specific - laws.

Under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, cancelled or "significantly delayed flights" - defined as three hours for domestic flights and six hours for international routes - must be offered alternative travel or a full refund of the fare if the passenger chooses not to fly.

It also requires all air carriers to issue refunds for tickets purchased with credit cards within seven business days of the request, and 20 days for tickets purchased with another form of payment. Passengers accepting a new flight cannot receive a refund.

In the US, there is no requirement for airlines to provide meal vouchers or accommodation, but some may offer complimentary support to customers.

However, if passengers are travelling from the UK to the US or flying with a UK carrier, you may have additional rights.

Under UK law, airlines have a duty to look after you when flights are delayed or cancelled for whatever reason.

a reasonable amount of food and drink (often through vouchers)

a way for you to communicate (often by refunding the cost of calls)

free accommodation, if you have to stay overnight to fly the next day

If your airline is unable to arrange assistance, you have the right to organise this yourself and claim back the cost later.

The Civil Aviation Authority advises people to keep receipts and not spend more than necessary.

It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001.

"This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.

Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system.

"That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.

The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published and flights were grounded until that system was restored.

Have you been affected by the US flight disruption? Tell us your story.

items.title: Dopo il caos nei cieli, Usa verso la 'piena operatività'. Ma si contano i danni
items.summary: Il blocco ha coinvolto quasi un milione e trecentomila persone
items.content:
Il caos del blocco totale di quasi 5 ore ai voli, deciso venerdì negli Stati Uniti, si è abbattuto anche sul sabato, nel mezzo degli sforzi per il ritorno alla normalità nei cieli americani. Ancora migliaia di cancellazioni e decine di migliaia di passeggeri rimasti intrappolati negli aeroporti, mentre, secondo le prime stime, il caos potrebbe aver causato danni per almeno un miliardo, tra spese extra sostenute dai viaggiatori e quelle delle compagnie aeree.

Le autorità hanno previsto che dei 41.000 voli americani programmati per l'intera giornata di oggi tra i 4.000 e i 5.000 sono probabilmente destinati ad essere cancellati, ha spiegato Bryan Bedford, amministratore della Federal Aviation Administration (Faa), l'agenzia americana che vigila sul traporto aereo. Anche se in tarda mattinata invece il numero delle cancellazioni aveva già raggiunto quota 4.600: un bilancio pesante, in aggiunta ai circa 9.000 voli commerciali soppressi venerdì, a cui aggiungere anche i 3.000 voli di jet privati, settore sempre in espansione. In definitiva, un bilancio non distante da quello della stessa Faa che già nella mattinata del 'day after' indicava più di 16.000 voli cancellati dall'inizio dell'emergenza.

Cifra impressionante, così come lo è la mole di passeggeri coinvolti: circa 1,1-1,3 milioni di persone, in gran parte nei principali scali americani, tra cui quelli di Boston, Atlanta, Miami, Pittsburgh, New York, Los Angeles e Baltimora. All'aeroporto internazionale John F. Kennedy di New York, a dispetto delle previsioni più ottimistiche, alcuni voli sono saltati a pochi minuti dall'inizio dell'imbarco: dagli altoparlanti è stato riferito che la causa era la carenza di personale, altro effetto collaterale del blocco.

Le compagnie, tra cui United, Delta e American, hanno fatto sapere che non applicheranno penali per la modifica dei biglietti. Gli aeroporti hanno invitato i passeggeri a verificare lo stato del proprio volo per evitare lunghe attese.

"Siamo tornati a piena operatività", ha assicurato il segretario ai Trasporti Sean Duffy, nel corso di una conferenza stampa: ma il ritorno alla normalità richiederà altro tempo, almeno tutto il fine settimana. L'obiettivo è riuscire ad assicurare la piena e totale regolarità dei voli per il Thanksgiving, la Giornata del Ringraziamento del 26 novembre, quando, grazie al ponte lungo, milioni di americani si metteranno in viaggio.

Le autorità americane indagano per far luce sul blocco dei voli che ha creato il caos e l'attenzione è tutta su alcune apparecchiature difettose, identificate e isolate, che hanno creato un effetto domino che ha portato al peggiore blocco aereo degli ultimi 25 anni, dai tempi degli attacchi terroristici alle Torri Gemelle dell'11 Settembre. A gennaio del 2023, a causa di un guasto al sistema della Federal Aviation Administration (Faa), era stato disposto un blocco dei voli nazionale per alcune ore, provocando ritardi nei collegamenti interni in tutto il Paese. All'epoca, la Faa spiegò che il sistema di notifica destinato al personale di volo era andato fuori uso durante la notte.

"Si tratta di una situazione assolutamente senza precedenti", ha commentato Robert Sumwalt, ex presidente del National Transportation Safety Board ed esperto di sicurezza dei trasporti. "Sono stato pilota di linea per 24 anni. Ero in volo l'11 Settembre; quella fu l'ultima volta in cui si verificò un blocco dei voli di tale portata. È davvero incredibile che una cosa del genere possa accadere al giorno d'oggi". Un'opinione ampiamente condivisa dalle decine di migliaia di persone intrappolate per il caos dei cieli a stelle e strisce, responsabile anche di pesanti disagi nei collegamenti con l'Europa.

items.title: SpaceX recupera per la prima volta nella storia un veicolo spaziale
items.summary: 'Si è inserito con precisione tra i bracci meccanici sulla rampa di lancio n.2'
items.content:
SpaceX di Elon Musk ha portato a termine con successo, per la prima volta nella storia, il recupero dello stadio superiore di un razzo orbitale convenzionale: la navetta Starship è rientrata in sicurezza sulla rampa di lancio dopo aver trascorso una giornata in orbita. Lo riferisce la Cnn, secondo cui il veicolo spaziale è riemerso da un cielo nuvoloso al termine di una discesa che ha attraversato il continente, inserendosi con precisione tra i bracci meccanici, soprannominati 'bacchette' (chopstick arms), situati sopra la rampa di lancio n.2. Si tratta di uno dei più grandi traguardi ingegneristici della storia aerospaziale.

Starship, alta 52 metri, ha completato con successo una manovra di atterraggio senza precedenti presso la torre di lancio 'Mechazilla', nel sud del Texas, in una impresa che è la prima nel suo genere. SpaceX ha avviato la missione, della durata prevista di 22 ore, venerdì pomeriggio a dispetto del blocco dei voli a terra imposto a livello nazionale dalla Faa per problemi emersi alle comunicazioni.

I razzi utilizzano sistemi di tracciamento e navigazione differenti da quelli usati dagli aeromobili: in una manovra senza precedenti, il veicolo spaziale Starship è sceso con estrema precisione, venendo accolto tra le braccia della torre di lancio 'Mechazilla' di SpaceX. Si tratta della prima volta nella storia dell'astronautica in cui lo stadio superiore di un razzo rientra dall'orbita effettuando un atterraggio sicuro in posizione verticale: un risultato che potrebbe aprire la strada a un suo futuro riutilizzo. Il successo di oggi giunge dopo che gli ingegneri di SpaceX avevano avvertito che l'azienda avrebbe potuto interrompere il tentativo in ogni momento, qualora fossero sorti dei problemi. I portavoce della società hanno sottolineato più volte che, data la natura dei rischi, i responsabili del volo avrebbero dovuto adottare un approccio prudente. Per raggiungere la torre di lancio, lo Starship ha dovuto sorvolare aree popolate del Texas e del Messico.

Durante la discesa, la Starship ha sfruttato le quattro piccole ali - o 'alette' - presenti sulla sua superficie esterna. "Durante il rientro, la Starship può modificare la propria traiettoria di volo muovendo le quattro alette di controllo. Ciò consente di mantenere un percorso sicuro e predefinito, guidandosi con estrema precisione verso Starbase", ha dichiarato SpaceX in un comunicato.

items.content: L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.

items.title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
items.summary: The US has not confirmed the Ukrainian president's comments - a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed".
items.content:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

The US has not confirmed Zelensky's comments, and a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".

The Ukrainian leader's comments came after US envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.

Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.

Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.

Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees that as unrealistic.

The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.

It is possible the American envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky said recently that the US mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.

Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.

So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public in order to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.

He maintains that the idea is now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security.

It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.

The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.

Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.

He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".

In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".

He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.

Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.

It has insisted again that it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal is in place that would include Ukraine ceding control of those parts of the Donbas Russian troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula Moscow annexed illegally in 2014.

The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.

Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service , which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.

Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine

US envoys meet Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Putin in Moscow

items.title: Nvidia deliberately kept GPU prices high through circular financing deals
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.techspot.com/news/114558-nvidia-deliberately-kept-gpu-prices-high-through-circular.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50501631 Points: 117 # Comments: 60
items.content:
Connecting the dots: The AI boom has been widely blamed for GPU prices spinning out of control over the past year. Following Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia,new information suggests that this was the goal of the former CEO's business strategy, which has long drawn accusations of circular financing.

A recent Wall Street Journal profile of Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress has shed more light on how Nvidia controversially financed its own customers to drive the AI boom. According to the report, the company pushed for more deals in mid-to-late 2026 to absorb an oversupply of TSMC wafers and keep GPU prices high.

Since at least last year, Nvidia has been accused of prolonging the AI boom by supporting the companies that buy its chips. Co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang, along with CFO Kress, even went so far as to defend the company against comparisons to Enron, which used similar tactics to illegally obscure its debt before its 2001 collapse.

Also read: GPU Prices Are Spiraling Out of Control - Q4 2026 Update

Behind the scenes, Kress expressed concern about the scale of the deals Nvidia had inked with cloud providers and major AI companies like OpenAI. Nvidia pushed ahead anyway, but by summer 2026, the company was wondering whether it had pushed too far amid an "avalanche" of semiconductors it had ordered from TSMC.

It was around this time that Huang berated Kress, calling her "a deer in headlights," according to someone familiar with the matter. Nvidia began to slow down, downsize, and pause some of its financing deals, including one with OpenAI that originally included a $250 billion backstop for the world's largest data center.

AI data centers have siphoned off DRAM and NAND manufacturing capacity traditionally used for RAM and storage in consumer devices, inflating prices. Nvidia's GeForce GPUs have been hit especially hard, with prices often exceeding 160% of their original MSRP. The company's flagship RTX 5090 has become unobtainable because Nvidia has directed its VRAM and semiconductors toward data center GPUs.

Colette Kress, Interim CEO and Executive VP and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) of Nvidia.

As its financial support deals wound down, Huang became worried about the company's stock market valuation, with its average monthly stock multiple falling far behind those of other large tech companies.

At a Berlin conference, the former CEO told major clients a story about a busy Japanese soup vendor who refused to give him a second serving after he had waited in a long line, saying the vendor had too many customers and not enough soup. Huang used the story to highlight the value of maintaining a diverse customer base and keeping prices high, suggesting that Nvidia's circular financing strategy inflated GPU prices by creating the perception of high demand.

The story emerged after Huang's resignation following the revelation of multiple extramarital affairs. One was with Alice Huang (no relation), whose company, Megaspeed, was suspected by US intelligence of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of export regulations. While some allege that she is a spy for Beijing, President Trump and the Justice Department said that hasn't been determined.

items.title: 'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
items.summary: SpaceX has performed the historic catch using mechanical arms nicknamed "chopsticks".
items.content:
SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time.

"Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas.

The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.

But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.

The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:20 local time (21:20 GMT) on Saturday, in the first-ever successful catch attempt.

Read more on this story: SpaceX successfully catches top of huge Starship rocket for first time

items.title: I bot si ribellano ai politici, 'colpa' di Microsoft down
items.summary: Messaggi da account sospetti. Salvini: 'Ci insultano'. Non si parli di hacker russi
items.content:
"Non posso scrivere un messaggio volto a insultare uno specifico partito politico" oppure "Non posso scrivere uno specifico messaggio finalizzato a convincere specifici eurodeputati a sostenere una proposta legislativa". Questi i messaggi comparsi nelle ultime ore e in modo massivo sulle pagine social di alcuni politici italiani, dal leader della Lega Matteo Salvini agli eurodeputati di FdI e Pd, Carlo Fidanza e Dario Nardella. La "rivolta dei bot contro i politici", la chiama Repubblica.it che mette in relazione i commenti seriali proveniente da "account sospetti" con il recente malfunzionamento di Microsoft e dei software di intelligenza artificiale (OpenAI e Anthropic).

La reazione della politica non si fa attendere, con il vicepremier Matteo Salvini che punta il dito: "Profili falsi arrivavano sui profili della Lega ad insultare e sulle pagine del Pd a glorificare. Vediamo chi c'è dietro. Voglio che siano le forze dell'ordine a capire. Spero che nessuno in questo caso tiri fuori gli hacker russi...". Ancor più duro il senatore Claudio Borghi secondo cui "è bastato un malfunzionamento per scoprire che, invece degli hacker russi, ci sono italianissimi personaggi ad inquinare il dibattito politico con schiere di bot addestrati per attaccare, guarda caso, la Lega e Matteo Salvini. In realtà la cosa non ci stupisce particolarmente: da tempo erano emerse notizie di squadre informatiche addestrate da PD, M5S e persino dalla UE per coordinare gli attacchi contro gli avversari politici". Ma anche Avs chiede chiarezza.

Angelo Bonelli riferisce di essere stato lui per primo vittima di questo fenomeno: "I miei profili sono costantemente assaliti da commenti minacciosi e insultanti". Di qui l'auspicio di un inchiesta della magistratura sulle "reti di account automatizzati che usano l'intelligenza artificiale per condizionare il dibattito politico". In questo caso "i bot, per errore, hanno pubblicato la risposta con cui l'IA si rifiutava di scrivere messaggi di propaganda o di insulti contro un partito.

items.title: Ucraina, Zelensky: 'Gli Usa ci propongono la Nato in cambio del Donbass'
items.summary: La Russia chiede il ritorno dell'Alleanza ai confini del 1997
items.content:
È il colpo di scena che potrebbe cambiare il quadro della situazione. Gli Stati Uniti - ha rivelato Volodymyr Zelensky una volta rientrato a Kiev dopo il tour de force diplomatico degli ultimi giorni - hanno per la prima volta evocato l'ipotesi che l'Ucraina possa entrare nella Nato in cambio della cessione dell'intero Donbass alla Russia. Il boccone sarebbe amaro da ingoiare.

È dal 2014 che Mosca cerca di conquistare gli oblast di Donetsk e Lugansk senza riuscirci -- uno scontro che è costato decine di migliaia di caduti da entrambi i lati. Gli ucraini a questo accetterebbero di cedere ulteriori territori per via diplomatica? Zelensky mette le mani avanti: servirebbe un "referendum". Il quadro è complicatissimo, siamo a migliaia di anni luce di distanza dalla partita di Natale a Risiko in famiglia. Intanto gli aspetti tecnici. Da quando scatterebbe l'ingresso nella Nato per Kiev, con la relativa protezione offerta dall'articolo 5? E gli Usa parlano davvero a nome di tutti? Sì perché per entrare nell'Alleanza serve l'unanimità. Ne sa qualcosa la Svezia, che pur avendo un pedigree cristallino sia in termini di valori democratici sia in capacità militari ha dovuto fare anticamera per due anni dalla richiesta d'ingresso a causa del veto della Turchia, a causa di questioni bilaterali.

Al vertice Nato di Vilnius, quando è stata coniata l'espressione "percorso irreversibile verso l'adesione", a mettere a freno i bollenti spiriti di Zelensky non sono stati solo gli Usa ma anche la Germania (e dietro Berlino si nascondevano pure altre capitali). Ecco perché non basta la parola e il presidente ucraino lo sa. "Ho ripetutamente affermato che l'Ucraina non si arrenderà e non cederà i suoi territori", ha detto Zelensky.

"Stiamo discutendo con i nostri partner un pacchetto di sicurezza completo che possono offrirci durante i negoziati: garanzie di sicurezza specifiche da parte della Nato e dell'Ue, un esercito ucraino forte, con un numero adeguato di soldati, armamenti, sostegno finanziario per un certo periodo di tempo, e il Piano di Prosperità, ovvero una roadmap di ripresa sostenuto da fondi con fonti chiare. Se la parte americana ce lo confermerà insieme agli altri colleghi della Nato, allora chiederò l'opinione della nostra società: lo accettiamo o no? Non ho il diritto di farlo a mia discrezione", ha precisato evidenziando che servono ancora "dettagli al momento non disponibili".

Peraltro manca ancora nell'equazione l'incognita Russia. Il Cremlino ha sempre avuto come obiettivo più o meno dichiarato l'esclusione dell'Ucraina dalla Nato, oltre che un ideale indebolimento dell'Alleanza: difficile che accetti. Un indizio forte viene dal documento negoziale che i russi hanno condiviso con gli americani ad Abu Dhabi, in cui hanno rievocato parte delle richieste avanzate nelle bozze di trattato del 2021. Ovvero, in primis, il ritiro delle truppe Nato dalle posizioni occupate nel 1997, prima che l'alleanza si espandesse. I funzionari russi - sostiene il New York Times, che ha visionato il materiale - hanno chiarito di considerare la Guerra Fredda e il Patto di Varsavia come un "modello" di architettura di sicurezza per l'Europa poiché le separate aree d'influenza statunitensi e sovietiche, così come gli accordi che ne derivavano, in realtà "riducevano" il rischio di conflitto.

Certo, rievocare il Patto di Varsavia nel 2026 appare una posizione lunare, che senz'altro farà drizzare i capelli in testa a tutto il fianco est europeo, Polonia e Baltici per primi. Ora che l'Europa ha finalmente trovato l'accordo sul suo team negoziale, con il neonato formato di Dublino (E5+Ue), si potrà senz'altro entrare di più nel dettaglio (a Berlino settimana prossima ci sarà un vertice della Coalizione dei Volenterosi, prima del grande trilaterale Putin-Trump-Xi in Cina). A Bruxelles, stamane, l'argomento più dibattuto nei salotti diplomatici è la 'labbrata' rifilata all'alto rappresentante Ue Kaja Kallas nella capitale irlandese, di fatto esautorata dal team negoziale. L'ex premier estone resta però il terminale di una filiera di Paesi europei decisi a non cedere alle richieste "folli" del Cremlino, convinti che ogni forma di appeasement genererà in futuro nuovi attacchi russi. Il Team Europe, nella sua sintesi, non potrà non tenerne conto, Kallas o meno. BGN

items.title: Maxi-multa del Garante per Meta, l'azienda prepara il ricorso
items.summary: Sanzione da 805 milioni per l'uso di foto "non autorizzato dell'utente" su Facebook
items.content:
Maxi-multa del Garante per la privacy, che ha inflitto a Meta una sanzione da 805 milioni di euro, pari a circa lo 0,47% del fatturato mondiale del gruppo. Al centro del provvedimento c'è l'app di Facebook per dispositivi Android, attraverso la quale la società avrebbe avuto accesso a fotografie, video e relativi metadati conservati negli smartphone degli utenti italiani senza aver ottenuto un consenso specifico né aver fornito un'informativa adeguata. Immediata la reazione del colosso statunitense, che ha annunciato ricorso.

Un portavoce di Meta ha dichiarato di essere "in netto disaccordo con la valutazione dei fatti e l'applicazione della normativa", giudicando la sanzione sproporzionata e ribadendo che si tratta di una semplice funzionalità di supporto alla pubblicazione, attivabile solo previa autorizzazione sul dispositivo e sempre modificabile dalle impostazioni. La vicenda ruota attorno alla funzione "Ottieni suggerimenti dalla galleria quando navighi su Facebook", introdotta nel 2023 per proporre contenuti presenti nella memoria del telefono come spunti pronti per la pubblicazione.

L'istruttoria, avviata nel luglio 2025 a seguito di una segnalazione del Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti di Bolzano, ha evidenziato gravi criticità tecniche: l'accesso alla galleria veniva richiesto tramite un'unica autorizzazione valida per l'intera applicazione, preceduta da un avviso generico ("abilitare altre funzioni") che non chiariva le reali finalità del trattamento. Inoltre, l'opzione risultava preimpostata come attiva, consentendo potenzialmente all'app di leggere l'intero archivio fotografico in modo permanente e senza possibilità di controllo da parte dell'utente o dell'Autorità. Secondo il Garante, tale meccanismo viola l'articolo 122 del Codice privacy (che recepisce la direttiva europea ePrivacy), norma che tutela lo smartphone come estensione della sfera privata della persona e impone un consenso libero e informato a prescindere dalla trasmissione dei dati o dall'esistenza di un danno.

L'Autorità ha inoltre respinto l'eccezione di incompetenza sollevata da Meta a favore dell'autorità irlandese, chiarendo che la disciplina ePrivacy non prevede il meccanismo dello "sportello unico". Sebbene il procedimento non abbia riguardato l'uso dei file per l'addestramento dell'intelligenza artificiale — pratica negata dall'azienda — il Garante si è riservato di effettuare accertamenti distinti sulla nuova funzione di elaborazione in cloud lanciata nel 2026. Nella quantificazione della multa hanno pesato l'ampia platea coinvolta (circa 20 milioni di utenti Android in Italia), la durata della violazione, un precedente provvedimento del 2019 e la scarsa collaborazione durante l'indagine. Elementi solo parzialmente mitigati da modifiche correttive giudicate tardive. Entro 60 giorni Meta dovrà mantenere la funzione disattivata di default, anche per chi aveva già dato l'ok, e introdurre una richiesta di consenso separata e trasparente; scaduto il termine, lo strumento dovrà essere bloccato per gli utenti privi di consenso valido. L'azienda avrà inoltre 30 giorni per comunicare le iniziative avviate e 90 giorni per rendicontare le misure adottate.

items.title: Francia, attacco alle Poste: hacker rubano i dati di 22 milioni di clienti
items.summary: Vittima a metà settembre la filiale Maileva, specializzata nella corrispondenza professionale
items.content:
Maileva, filiale del gruppo La Poste specializzata nell’invio di corrispondenza professionale, è stata vittima di un grave attacco informatico a metà settembre, che ha portato al furto dei dati personali di 22 milioni di persone. Lo ha reso noto ieri La Poste all’agenzia Afp. Maileva «ha notificato l’accaduto alla Cnil», l’autorità garante per la protezione dei dati, e ha sporto denuncia: «È in corso un’indagine giudiziaria», ha aggiunto La Poste, confermando quanto riportato dai siti specializzati FrenchBreaches e cyberattaque.org, secondo i quali si tratta di «una delle più grandi fughe di dati in Francia». Maileva – specializzata nella corrispondenza professionale per pmi e imprese di medie dimensioni – conta oltre 70mila utenti e nel 2024 ha gestito l’invio di 180 milioni di documenti.

L’attacco subito «ha comportato l’esposizione dei dati personali (nome, cognome, indirizzo postale) di 22 milioni di persone, destinatari della corrispondenza inviata per conto delle aziende clienti di Maileva», precisa il gruppo La Poste in una dichiarazione.

L’anno scorso, a pochi giorni da Natale, La Poste era già stata colpita da un attacco informatico, rivendicato da hacker filorussi.

items.title: Sondaggio, 'Le Pen nettamente in testa, Mélenchon secondo, Riner al 4,5%'
items.summary: La rilevazione di Elabe realizzata per Bfmtv e La Tribune Dimanche
items.content:
Marine Le Pen si conferma saldamente in testa nelle intenzioni di voto per il primo turno delle presidenziali, davanti a Jean-Luc Mélenchon, che si colloca al secondo posto; in calo invece Édouard Philippe e Raphaël Glucksmann, mentre Teddy Riner è accreditato del 4,5%, secondo un sondaggio Elabe pubblicato oggi.

Nello studio, realizzato per Bfmtv e La Tribune Dimanche, la candidata del Rassemblement National resta nettamente in vantaggio, attestandosi su valori sostanzialmente stabili tra il 31% e il 33%, a seconda degli scenari presi in esame. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, esponente de La France Insoumise, guadagna tra 1,5 e 2 punti percentuali e si porta in seconda posizione, con una percentuale di consensi compresa tra il 17% e il 18,5%.

Il suo risultato migliore si registra in assenza di Marine Tondelier e François Ruffin. Édouard Philippe perde 1,5 punti: il candidato di Horizons ottiene il 15% (a 2 punti di distanza da Jean-Luc Mélenchon) qualora non siano in lizza Gabriel Attal e David Lisnard, ma siano presenti Bruno Retailleau e Dominique de Villepin. La sua percentuale scende al 12% se anche Gabriel Attal è tra i candidati, e al 13% se è presente David Lisnard (in assenza di Attal). Il dato scende ulteriormente al 9,5% nello scenario che prevede il maggior numero di candidati.

items.title: Uomo di 92 anni ucciso durante una truffa del falso carabiniere
items.summary: I due fermati gli fecero scrivere appunto; in intercettazioni, "non l'ho spinto forte"
items.content:
Doveva essere l'ennesima truffa nei confronti di un anziano, una delle tante che avvengono ogni giorno e in ogni parte d'Italia, ma questa volta è finita nel peggiore dei modi con la morte di un pensionato di 92 anni. Quella tentata il 27 ottobre nella casa dell'uomo a Milano con la tecnica del "falso carabiniere" è infatti diventata prima una rapina e poi un omicidio per il quale sono stati fermati due giovani egiziani, di 19 e 24 anni. La morte dell'anziano, ex tecnico dell'Alfa Romeo che abitava da solo in un appartamento in via Muratori, era stata scoperta dalla figlia e sembrava dovuta a cause accidentali, ma l'autopsia ha evidenziato lesioni alla testa non compatibili con una caduta.

Sono subito le indagini con gli agenti e i funzionari della Squadra Mobile che hanno cominciato a raccogliere elementi, iniziando dalle telecamere dei negozi vicine. Gli agenti della Squadra mobile hanno trovato sul tavolo della cucina un "elemento di riscontro probatorio inestimabile: un foglio manoscritto la cui calligrafia era riconducibile a quello della vittima". Sul foglio le annotazioni: "non in possesso di alcun indumento legato al colpo" e "non possesso di armi legato al colpo". Un elemento, riportato nel fermo del pm che dimostrerebbe "in modo altamente emblematico l'avvenuta sottomissione psicologica dell'anziano, presumibilmente calzante" con il piano della truffa finita in tragedia. Vi è poi la cronologia delle telefonate rilevate in entrata sul telefono cellulare (trovato dagli investigatori). Risultano chiamate dopo le 13 del 27 ottobre (Re morì il giorno dopo in ospedale) di otto minuti, una poi dei 23 minuti. Poco prima che uno dei due fermati si presentasse alla sua porta. A carico dei due anche delle intercettazioni fatte in questura: "Non l'ho spinto forte" e "non parlare troppo con gli investigatori".

Vicini e negozianti hanno da subito collaborato alle indagini, mettendo a disposizione le immagini, ma anche raccontando che cosa avevano visto. E anche oggi ricordano che "non c'erano segni di scasso sulla porta: gli ha aperto lui". Nel tentativo di truffa sfociato in tragedia uno dei due fermati avrebbe avuto il ruolo di "palo", e ci sono le immagini a documentarlo, mentre l'altro si sarebbe introdotto nella casa dell'anziano aggredendolo con violenza e impossessandosi di gioielli e altri oggetti di valore. Ora gli investigatori e la Procura che ha disposto il fermo per omicidio e rapina aggravata sono convinti di avere elementi solidi nei confronti dei due giovani che non hanno parlato davanti al gip nell'udienza di convalida e restano in carcere in attesa che il giudice decida se debbano rimanerci, come chiesto dai pm. I due erano stati arrestati una decina di giorni dopo la morte dell'anziano milanese dalla Polizia in provincia di Varese per una tentata truffa ai danni di una donna di 81 anni. Il copione era stato lo stesso del 27 ottobre con una sola variante: si erano spacciati per militari della Guardia di Finanza e il bottino era stato di monili in oro per 50 mila euro.

Erano stati rimessi in libertà dopo l'udienza di convalida, con l'obbligo di firma alla Polizia giudiziaria, prima che si scoprisse il loro coinvolgimento nell'omicidio del pensionato milanese. Nelle indagini sull'omicidio gli investigatori stanno lavorando per stabilire quanto i due truffatori seriali avessero una rete che preparava il loro ingresso in campo quasi a colpo sicuro, come accade molto spesso nelle truffe telefoniche agli anziani. Lo dimostrano un tentativo di truffa da parte due finte poliziotte arrestate per aver preso 200.000 euro a un pensionato a Roma e altri due arresti a Udine in un'operazione da parte della Squadra Mobile di Padova dopo un'altra truffa del finto carabiniere.

items.title: Finito l'incubo per l'italiano Echenagucia, in cella in Venezuela dal 2024
items.summary: Era accusato di terrorismo. A giugno l'allarme dell'Osa sulla sua salute
items.content:
È finita oggi la lunga detenzione di Daniel Enrique Echenagucia Vallenilla, imprenditore italo-venezuelano originario dell'Avellinese, scarcerato dopo oltre due anni in cella in Venezuela. Ad annunciare la notizia è stata la Farnesina precisando che Echenagucia dopo essere stato scarcerato "è stato accolto presso il Consolato Generale d'Italia a Caracas".

Il vicepremier e ministro degli Esteri Antonio Tajani ha commentato positivamente la sua scarcerazione, precisando che il rilascio "segna un altro passo avanti nel processo di transizione democratica intrapreso dal Venezuela: confermo la disponibilità italiana ad accompagnare - anche come membro dell'Unione Europea - questo percorso".

Echenagucia era stato arrestato il 2 agosto 2024 ad un posto di blocco della Guardia nazionale bolivariana a Valencia, nello Stato di Carabobo, mentre viaggiava in auto con la moglie e i due figli. Secondo il rapporto dell'organizzazione non governativa Foro Penal, che monitora la situazione dei detenuti politici nel Paese sudamericano, gli erano stati contestati i reati di cospirazione, associazione per delinquere, terrorismo, finanziamento del terrorismo e tradimento della patria.

Dopo il fermo era stato trasferito nella sede del controspionaggio militare (Dgcim) a Caracas e successivamente nel carcere di Rodeo I, nello Stato di Miranda. Il procedimento giudiziario a suo carico ha subito ripetuti rinvii, fino alla svolta di oggi.

La sua liberazione è avvenuta dopo che le autorità giudiziarie hanno disposto la sostituzione della detenzione con misure cautelari, accogliendo una raccomandazione dell'associazione Programma per la Convivenza Democratica e la Pace. La sua situazione era stata segnalata anche dalla Commissione interamericana dei diritti umani (Cidh), organismo dell'Organizzazione degli Stati Americani (Osa), che aveva segnalato il rischio di danni alla sua vita, alla sua integrità e alla sua salute, citando presunte aggressioni, limitazioni nei contatti con l'esterno e la mancanza di cure adeguate per diverse patologie, tra cui asma cronico, artrosi e ipertensione.

Il Programma per la Convivenza Democratica e la Pace ha accolto la scarcerazione come un passo a sostegno del dialogo e della riconciliazione nazionale, richiamando l'impegno della presidente ad interim Delcy Rodriguez per la convivenza democratica e la pace, nel rispetto delle leggi del Paese.

Dopo la scarcerazione del cooperante Alberto Trentini, liberato il 12 gennaio 2026 dopo 423 giorni di detenzione insieme all'imprenditore Mario Burlò, non risulterebbero più cittadini con il solo passaporto italiano detenuti in Venezuela. Restano invece decine di casi che riguardano italo-venezuelani. Un dossier consegnato nell'agosto scorso dai familiari al deputato eletto nella circoscrizione esteri per il Sudamerica, Fabio Porta, indicava tra i nomi di detenuti José Luongo, Juan Carlos Marrufo, Gerardo Cotticchia, Olvany Gasperi, Tulio Medina Gianfelice, Walter e Massimiliano Ranieri, Carmelo, Daniel e Levin De Grazia e Daniel Necol Buttafuoco. Resta infine irrisolto il caso di Hugo Enrique Marino Salas, scomparso nell'aprile 2019 dopo essere stato prelevato, secondo la famiglia, da agenti del controspionaggio militare venezuelano, senza che da allora si siano più avute sue notizie.

items.title: 'Miracle on Mississippi' - All passengers rescued after New Orleans cruise ship collision
items.summary: The collision leaves 32 people in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for.
items.content:
Some 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker.

The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel Atlantic Asphalt.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".

The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Capt Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference on Friday that all credit in the rescue effort should go to first responders who "literally jumped right in to help".

"We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," Moreno said.

Calls about the collision began around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday, when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans chief Melanie Montroll told the news conference.

Were you in the area at the time of incident? Get in touch .

There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.

Passengers began getting off the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping onto its side, Moreno said.

Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.

The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

On Saturday, Moreno said that nine people are still in hospital.

She said that the captain of the ship was injured in the accident but refused medical treatment until he knew all passengers and crew were accounted for.

US President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the rescue had been an "incredible job".

Governor Jeff Landry also hailed the rescue as a "miracle on the Mississippi" given the "sheer number of people who were on that cruise ship" who were rescued.

Ships have operated safely on the Mississippi River for years, Landry said, pledging to investigate what had occurred.

Still covered in dirt from the boat crash, Joe Knab of Kansas told New Orleans NBC affiliate WDSU that the ship quickly capsized after the collision.

He spent about 20 minutes in the water before being rescued.

"When we first went in we were bobbing underneath the water; it was sinking pretty fast, but we finally got out of there," he said.

Jamie Holford, a witness to the crash, told the BBC's US partner CBS that he had seen the cruise ship hit the dock following the collision.

"It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like," he said. "It looked like something off the Titanic."

Holford added that he had seen passengers and crew "hollering" and "crying" as they tried to get off the ship while it was sinking.

The American Heritage can carry up to 150 guests and features a glass-enclosed restaurant, fitness centre and three guest lounges, according to its website.

If you were in the area at the time of the incident, please get in touch.

items.title: Il Papa dalle Ande: 'Mai cedere alla violenza, non è la via per il progresso'
items.summary: 'Migrazioni forzate e sfruttamento iniquo delle risorse del suolo sfide che preoccupano'
items.content:
"Pensiamo in questi luoghi alla sofferenza di chi è costretto ad abbandonare la propria terra per cercare un futuro migliore, per sé e per i propri cari, nelle grandi città costiere; o alle difficoltà di ricambio generazionale legate al fenomeno della denatalità, che svuotano i paesi; o alla sfida dell'equa condivisione dei benefici legati alle risorse del suolo. Di fronte a tante criticità, si può essere tentati di cedere allo scoraggiamento, al risentimento, o addirittura alla violenza, ma questa non sarà mai la via del progresso e della pace".

Papa Leone raggiunge la sua terza tappa significativa in Perù, quella parrocchia di Santa Cruz situata a oltre 2mila metri di altezza sulla cordigliera delle Ande, un luogo remoto dove si arriva imboccando sentieri impervi o su per la accidentata 'carretera' tra curve spigolose e pendii scoscesi, dove si nasconde però un tesoro di tradizioni, devozione popolare, cultura andina e tracce della civiltà Inca su cui vuole attirare i riflettori del mondo.

Un concentrato di storia e cultura che conosce di prima mano, dai tempi in cui vescovo missionario lui stesso impiegava quattro ore di macchina per salire fin qui a celebrare. Oggi, da Papa, sono bastati 40 minuti di elicottero. "Vengo tra voi come missionario" esordisce dopo aver consacrato all' Immacolata della cattedrale di Chiclayo il suo intero ministero petrino, "qui la fede valorizza la terra, il lavoro onesto e la famiglia" che rappresentano un "antidoto salutare alla superficialità e al consumismo oggi dilaganti".

"Anche oggi le tenebre continuano a essere in agguato e sembrano avvolgerci completamente", aveva detto in mattinata. Anche per questo, pur se "ci sentiamo minacciati dall'incertezza della violenza diffusa, dalla sofferenza indicibile che continua a colpire tanti fratelli", "l'egoismo, l'ingiustizia e la malvagità - sottolinea il Pontefice - non si sconfiggono con la brutalità, ma con la preghiera, con la pazienza, con la perseveranza nel denunciare ciò che non va, chiedendo con forza e lavorando con impegno affinché si realizzino i cambiamenti necessari".

"C'è uno stretto legame - incoraggia quindi il popolo dei 20mila accorsi anche percorrendo sentieri di montagna - tra fede, preghiera e azione. Dove c'è fede, c'è preghiera, e dove c'è preghiera, c'è capacità di impegno per gli altri. Voi, abitanti di queste terre, lo sapete bene. Nonostante molte difficoltà, non avete mai perso la fiducia in voi stessi. È la fede che vi rende grandi nelle vostre aspirazioni e nei vostri progetti".

"In proposito - conclude -, vorrei lodare chi, con ingegnosità e intraprendenza, si adopera a dare lavoro dignitoso alle persone: contadini, commercianti, piccoli imprenditori e tanti altri che qui, giorno per giorno, impiegano i talenti ricevuti a favore delle comunità, contribuendo a promuovere, con l'occupazione, autentici modelli di sviluppo umano integrale".

items.title: Dartmouth (Guarini) will not admit math PhD cohort this year
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.thedartmouth.com/article/2026/11/gandhi-fagell-guarini-will-not-admit-math-ph-d-cohort-this-year Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50499945 Points: 67 # Comments: 25
items.content:
The Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies has suspended admissions to the next cohort in its math Ph.D. program, which would matriculate in the 2027-2028 academic year. Guarini dean Carrie Colla ’01 and College spokesperson Jana Barnello did not specify when or whether the program would resume admissions.

Colla wrote in a Nov. 10 email statement to The Dartmouth that Guarini “regularly considers how to best invest in graduate education.”

“As part of those regular reviews, we are pausing admissions to the math Ph.D. program for the 2027-2028 cycle while the School of Arts and Sciences conducts a department review,” she wrote.

The decision to suspend the program “was made in close partnership with leaders in the School of Arts and Sciences and we look forward to working collaboratively with the department on this review,” Colla added.

She wrote in a Nov. 10 email to current graduate students that there “will be opportunities for students to participate in the review” and that she would meet with math graduate students and department faculty on Nov. 17. Graduate students can also reach out to math department chair Dimitrios Giannakis and math professor Vladimir Chernov to share questions and concerns, she wrote.

“While I know it is disappointing news that your cohort will not be growing next year, I am confident that this approach will allow us to strengthen the experience of both our Ph.D. students and the undergraduate students in the department,” Colla wrote.

During a Q&A at the Nov. 9 general faculty meeting, which The Dartmouth attended but was not permitted to record, faculty raised concerns about the suspension. Math professor Peter Winkler, who opposed the suspension, said at the meeting the decision was communicated to math department faculty on Nov. 6. Winkler declined to provide additional comment after the meeting.

The Ph.D. program’s pause follows a national trend of decreasing Ph.D. program seats. Data collected from 55 undisclosed research institutions demonstrated that Ph.D. acceptances dropped 15% in 2026 from the previous year, even though domestic applications increased.

In a Nov. 10 email to current graduate students, which was obtained and reviewed by The Dartmouth, Giannakis wrote that faculty members were “continuing to engage” with College administrators to “find a path forward” that would “eventually resume” the Ph.D. program.

Giannakis added in the email that Colla and School of Arts and Sciences dean Nina Pavcnik would attend a math department faculty meeting on Nov. 11 to discuss the suspension. “While I do not expect a reversal of the decision to pause admissions, I hope there will at least be a constructive dialogue with actionable outcomes,” he wrote.

The Guarini admissions office communicated the decision to applicants on Nov. 10, according to an email obtained by The Dartmouth. Any materials or recommendation letters that have already been submitted “will not be reviewed,” the Guarini admissions office wrote. Applications for the program, which typically accepts seven to nine students per year, would have been due on Dec. 15, 2026, according to the math department website .

“We recognize this is disappointing news and we are sorry for the disruption to your plans,” the email to people who already submitted application materials reads. On Nov. 10, Colla wrote to current math graduate students that “status and support” for current students “are not changing” and that the program will see “every currently enrolled student through graduation,” according to an email obtained and reviewed by The Dartmouth.

“Stipends, insurance and the five-year funding guarantee all remain in place for students making satisfactory academic progress,” Colla wrote. “Advising relationships, qualifying exams, degree requirements and teaching and research appointments will continue as planned.”

Guarini Ph.D. students received an annual stipend of $49,862.40 for the 2026-2027 academic year, along with tuition remission, health insurance and other benefits, according to the Guarini website. The College guarantees five years of financial support to students making satisfactory academic progress. Graduate students typically teach “one course in each of their final three years of study,” according to the math department graduate student handbook. Starting this term, math Ph.D. candidates must also serve as a teaching assistant for one term each year after their third year, while first and second-year Ph.D. candidates must serve as teaching assistants for three terms a year instead of the previously required two, according to the handbook.

Third-year math Ph.D. candidate Jacob Lehmann Duke GR said he and his fellow graduate students learned of the suspension from Colla’s Nov. 10 email. He said he was “frustrated” by the “lack of transparency” surrounding the decision. “We were all shocked,” he said. “There was no indication that this was coming.”

Second-year math Ph.D. candidate Alex Moon GR said they believe suspending applications for the upcoming cycle sends “a message of instability” to future applicants.

“Part of the deal of graduate school is that you want there to be minimal factors outside of your control that will prevent you from getting this Ph.D.,” Moon said. “If this is something they do once, it’s something they can do later.”

In an interview with The Dartmouth, second-year math Ph.D. candidate Aidan Hennessey GR said “losing out on a cohort of students” would negatively affect the discussions among the “already quite small” Ph.D. program.

“Having people in adjacent areas of math to you — that you can talk about math and learn from, teach and talk through ideas with — all of this is very helpful,” Hennessey said. “Having more students around is nice for community.”

Lehmann Duke added that the suspension could put undergraduates intending to enroll in graduate-level mathematics courses “at a real deficit.”

Ben Singer ’27 — who said they have taken graduate-level math courses since their freshman year — added that there are “a few core graduate courses” that are “really important for undergraduates here who want to get into graduate school.” A decrease in Ph.D. students raises questions about whether those classes will be offered, whether undergraduates will be able to take them and how fewer course offerings will affect people who want to go to graduate school, Singer said.

The College “reserves the right to make changes in the offering” or cancel a course with fewer than five enrolled students, according to the Arts and Sciences Registrar’s Office website.

First-year computational science and modeling Ph.D. candidate Ethan Baird GR said “almost half” of his program’s coursework requirements are typically fulfilled through mathematics department courses. Baird added that these classes are the “basis of everything that we end up doing later,” which leads him to worry that the suspension of the admissions will have trickle-down effects on the computational science and modeling Ph.D. programs. Math major Ribhu Hooja ’27 said the department “did not officially” inform undergraduate students about the pause and that he instead found out from graduate students. If the pause lasts “even for a year, there could still be harm” because of “the relationships formed” between undergraduate and graduate students in advanced math classes, Hooja said.

“We learn how to apply to grad school, and what it means,” Hooja said. “It’s an important relationship I’ve really benefitted a lot from.”

Third-year Ph.D. candidate Michaela Polley GR said she was concerned about the pause’s effects on “research culture” among Dartmouth graduates and undergraduates alike.

“The idea of being a research university and a liberal arts college doesn’t work if you don’t have graduate students,” she said.

During the Nov. 9 meeting, College President Sian Leah Beilock and Pavcnik also addressed faculty concerns about the College’s discontinuation of the Society of Fellows, a three-year interdisciplinary research program established in 2014 to support postdoctoral research and scholarship. The Society has stopped recruiting new fellows and will conclude in summer 2028, when its current cohort completes their appointments, according to the program’s website. Beilock said at the meeting that the decision follows the need to reinvest funding in other institutional priorities.

Beilock announced at the meeting that the College is “working to reduce Dartmouth’s spending by $50 million,” in order to increase faculty and staff salaries “especially if and when inflation continues to rise,” according to a transcript of her speech published on the Office of the President’s website .

In a Nov. 11 email statement to The Dartmouth, Barnello wrote that the $50 million “reflects adjustments already made” to the budget, and that “roughly half” is “already in place” for fiscal year 2027.

Beilock also announced at the meeting that the College is “preparing” to convert North Park apartments, which are currently listed on the Office of Residential Life website as undergraduate housing, to graduate student housing. The North Park apartments have exclusively housed undergraduates since the 2022-2023 academic year, according to the Dartmouth Graduate Student Council website .

items.title: Copper wire upgrade caused nationwide flight suspension, US transport secretary says
items.summary: The US government is trying to find out whether the chaos was caused by "incompetence" or faulty equipment.
items.content:
A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said.

Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment.

The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said.

Friday's suspension was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US and the disruption is expected to last for days.

Maintenance was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider company, Duffy said.

The US has "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he added.

"It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued," he said.

The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes which led the government to shut down the airspace for safety reasons.

Bryan Bedford, who heads the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI related."

On Saturday L3Harris said it had completed over 70% of the work to modernise communications infrastructure before the shutdown.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel," it said in a statement.

"L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."

No flights were allowed to take off from the continental US for more than four hours from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday.

More than 3,500 flights were cancelled and more than 2,000 delayed in the US on Saturday, according to tracking website Flight Aware, as knock-on disruption continues.

In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. Some international flights were allowed to depart US airports, in an apparent effort to clear space.

Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure.

US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party.

Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?"

A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks.
